I’m watching three friends lose 11 lbs of body weight in a race car tomorrow

+ Tobias Lutke (founder shopify)
+ DHH (creator ruby on rails)
+ Mathias Beche (le mans podium)
 
Race car driving is insane… 

+ 122°F cockpit
+ heart rate 170
+ 2.5 hours straight
+ 10 hr race 
+ up to 4.2 g force (wild)
+ multi-layer fireproof suit
+ sweat barely evaporate
+ 600-900 calories per hour

The race is a 10-hour endurance track in atlanta.  It’s called Motul Petit Le Mans. 

Tomorrow is the season finale, where 54 cars across multiple classes run roughly 400 laps of the 2.54-mile road. The race doesn’t end till 10 pm.

They’ll be driving an LMP2: 
+ 603 horsepower
+ 2,050 pounds
+ 9,000 rpm

I’ve personally experienced some of the above things:

> core body temp of 102°F
> 3 g force in my airplane 
> non evaporative clothing 
> stomping 200 lbs
> severe dehydration

But never all at once… inside a race car for 2.5 hours straight, competing for tenths of a second, and in a high risk environment. 

I’m struggling to get my head around it.

Last week, Tobi and I were at a conference catching up. He and I have been friends for 15 years. 

Tobi and DHH were my first customers at my payments startup Braintree.  I’ll forever be grateful to them and DHH’s co-founder

Tobi approaches racing as I do my body. Data, method and analysis. A closed loop game of continuous improvement.

Off the track, Tobi:

+ 20 yrs building

Off the track, DHH:

On the track, Mathias Beche:

hits.name: Andy Galpin, PhD
hits.text:
Why wouldn't you want your testosterone as high as possible? Dr. Ben House has a good answer.

High testosterone upregulates EPO, which tells your body to make more red blood cells. More red blood cells means more viscous blood. You're not pumping blood anymore, you're pumping oil.

Now add left ventricular hypertrophy. The heart wall thickens, and it's pushing against more back pressure with every beat.

As Ben puts it, your heart is pumping ketchup against a bunch of extra muscle.

You don't want to run that for decades, assuming you get decades.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Exercise slowed epigenetic aging on two DNA-methylation clocks in breast cancer survivors.

During the first 6 months of the 12-month study, epigenetic aging halted in the exercise group while controls aged at twice the chronological rate, even though the intervention added only about 6 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity per day!

Faster epigenetic aging was also associated with worse attention and self-reported cognition, and some methylation changes implicated BDNF signaling as a plausible link to neuroplasticity.

This suggests some aging signatures after cancer treatment appear to be responsive to movement, even when the added activity isn't enormous.

hits.text:
It’s a reality of aging that we need more dietary protein to keep muscle mass. If you're over 65, the source of your protein may matter as much as the amount.

Researchers gave older adults two meals with the same amount of protein and the same calories. One was built around beef, and the other was vegan. After the beef meal, muscle protein synthesis was about 47% higher. After the vegan meal, it barely moved from where it was before eating (PMID 37972895).

As we age, muscle gets harder to build and easier to lose. We need to make high-quality animal protein the anchor of every meal.

Want to explore a topic from one of my letters? Ask a follow-up question about a video? Dig deeper into the science of metabolism, nutrition, or longevity?

outsiders.name: Andrej Karpathy
outsiders.text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

outsiders.name: Atal
outsiders.text:
The anatomy of an AI agent, explained simply:

1. Perception: Receives input from users, APIs, files, or sensors.
Example: You ask an agent to summarize your emails.

2. Reasoning: The LLM understands the request and decides what to do next.

3. Planning: Breaks a complex task into smaller steps.
Example: Find emails → identify important ones → summarize them.

4. Memory: Stores conversation context and retrieves relevant past information.

5. Tool execution: Uses APIs, MCP, databases, browsers, or code to perform actions.

6. Guardrails: Controls permissions, checks risky actions, and requests human approval when needed.

7. Observability: Tracks logs, errors, latency, and costs so developers can debug the agent.

How it works:
Input → Reason → Plan → Use tools → Check results → Repeat until the task is complete.

An AI agent isn't just an LLM. It's a system that combines models, tools, memory, and control mechanisms to get things done.

virals.name: Andrej Karpathy
virals.text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

In physics, an “impedance mismatch” occurs when two systems each work well but are poorly matched.

In this Science Blog guest post, Harvard physicist Matthew Schwartz argues that something similar is happening with AI and science. LLMs are capable at many things, but working with them as you would with a human collaborator isn’t currently the best way to elicit their scientific strengths.

To address this mismatch, Schwartz created a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science. Because similar calculations often emerge in very different areas of science, Claude found connections to ecology, population genetics, and a dozen other fields, and Schwartz worked with domain experts to steer it towards interesting questions.

i couldn't sleep after reading this

Sam Altman just explained how he uses his own AI agent, and it feels illegal:

he leaves it one long voice note as he's drifting off. by morning the thing is built, and it already "did the next seven steps"

his agent is called Dotty. it sorts the morning fires and only pings him when something is urgent. in his words, it gave him "space for creativity or to just hang out with my kids"

that's literally what openai dots does now. the launch post hit 13.7 million views three days ago. each dot gets its own computer in the cloud, plugs into 4,000+ apps, and you message it inside chatgpt, slack or teams. your laptop stays shut

getting the same morning out of your own dot takes five moves, and the first one matters most:

→ give it one job and keep the chain short. in openai's own safety tests, handing a dot 10 tasks in a row instead of 5 more than doubled the slip-ups
→ write the brief as four answers: what must get done, which sources it reads, what deserves your attention, what it must not do yet
→ skip scheduling the follow-ups. it can "decide when to pause and wake up to continue work", so give it the goal and let it pick its own hours
→ ask for a handful of versions. Altman leaves Dotty notes on how a feature should work and gets several builds back to pick from
→ write repeat jobs like a calendar invite: "every friday at 17:00, post the summary in the team channel. only what's in the summary. ask me first before posting anywhere else"

dots are live on chatgpt pro and business premium, and your first dot comes included in the plan

it learns from your feedback over time. six months from now, the people who started this week will have a dot that knows how they work, and everyone else starts from zero

full playbook in my article below. bookmark this before tonight's voice note

holy sh*t. Sam Altman shows his personal dots setup

one dot. one job. it works the night shift so he doesn't have to:

-> reads everything that came in overnight: email, calendar, Slack, DMs
-> sorts it into urgent vs can wait, based on how he likes to work
-> drafts the replies and sends nothing
-> checks every action against his custom rules: proceed, ask him, or hand it off

-> it reaches him in ChatGPT, Slack, Teams or by call
-> whatever he edits or ignores goes back into memory

runs 24/7 on its own cloud computer, through plug-ins he already connected

how i'd copy it:

> read-only for a week
> sending always asks
> correct it out loud

included in Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise

give yours the night shift tonight

virals.name: Mr. Buzzoni
virals.text:
Claude Code tip: before you ship a vibe-coded site, let Opus 5.5 send 𝟱 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 through 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝟮𝟬 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀 and fix everything in one pass:

1. design that holds together
• write a DESIGN file first and tie every color, font size, spacing and radius to it
• keep the palette tight and the type hierarchy clear
• same kind of button, card or input = same look
• flat page? add emphasis. crowded page? cut
• text stays readable on dark and light backgrounds

2. mobile
• nothing scrolls sideways or spills off screen
• add a real mobile menu
• buttons big enough for a thumb
• the layout survives enlarged text

3. every state
• loading, empty and error each get a proper screen
• every button gets its own hover, pressed and disabled look
• form errors show up next to the field, plus submitting, success and failure messages
• modals, dropdowns and tabs switch with transitions

4. click it like a real user
• run sign-up and checkout from start to finish
• hunt down dead buttons and broken links
• make sure the whole site works with just a keyboard

5. pre-launch
• the home page says what you do in one line
• each page gets one main button
• every page has a title, a description and a favicon
• delete every bit of placeholder text

on effort: Anthropic's cost guide puts medium on well-scoped daily work, so the default covers these 20 fixes
raise it only for the hard ones - Thariq's tests showed higher effort mostly buys extra verification and edge-case testing

paste this whole post into Claude Code and add this at the end 

"Run a pre-ship check on this repo.

You: main session, Opus 5.5, medium effort.
Spawn 5 read-only subagents, one per group:

design (medium) - DESIGN file, styles/globals.css, tailwind.config.ts, components/ui/
mobile (medium) - app/layout.tsx, components/nav/, every page at 375px
states (medium) - components/forms/, every loading, empty and error view
real user (high) - app/signup/, app/checkout/, every link and button
launch (medium) - app/page.tsx, page metadata, public/favicon.ico

Each subagent:
- checks only its group
- edits nothing
- returns issue, file:line, severity

Then:
1. merge all five lists into .claude/preship/issues.json, grouped by file, no duplicates
2. stop and show me the list - no edits until I confirm
3. after I confirm, fix everything yourself in one pass, so no two agents touch the same file
4. save before and after screenshots to .claude/preship/screens/"

virals.name: Atal
virals.text:
The anatomy of an AI agent, explained simply:

1. Perception: Receives input from users, APIs, files, or sensors.
Example: You ask an agent to summarize your emails.

2. Reasoning: The LLM understands the request and decides what to do next.

3. Planning: Breaks a complex task into smaller steps.
Example: Find emails → identify important ones → summarize them.

4. Memory: Stores conversation context and retrieves relevant past information.

5. Tool execution: Uses APIs, MCP, databases, browsers, or code to perform actions.

6. Guardrails: Controls permissions, checks risky actions, and requests human approval when needed.

7. Observability: Tracks logs, errors, latency, and costs so developers can debug the agent.

How it works:
Input → Reason → Plan → Use tools → Check results → Repeat until the task is complete.

An AI agent isn't just an LLM. It's a system that combines models, tools, memory, and control mechanisms to get things done.
